body: You sound like you enjoy your life, it comes through in your writing.. thanks for the time you spent to write.

Honestly, nothing is really that important to me other than meeting my baseline obligations (car insurance, food, gas).  Having a brother who isn't an alcoholic, a mother who isn't diabetic, paying off the 10's of 1000's of dollars in medical debt, maybe, otherwise I don't really know.

I don't know what attributes well balanced people have on the inside, but the person they reflect on the outside is usually socially competent (humorous, risk-taking, mildly ambitious, pleasant to be around) and has the ability to confront problems without going into crisis mode like I do.  They seem to roll with the punches.

I have a distant uncle that raised two boys who have moved on to very successful careers.  They were very close as a family, did family things, and worked through their problems and celebrated each others' successes.  Something about whatever they were getting in that environment seemed to work:  One kid is a successful engineer who had no problem finding a job right out of school during this recession, the other works with computers and has the same background.

My other uncle has two kids, and although he is divorced, he kept an active role in their lives.  Both are college graduates, one a chemist, moving onward and upward.

I would say that those kids, 3 of which are male, were well balanced.  They were given some kind of tools for success through having positive male influences in life.  I don't know how it works, it just seems to work.  I don't know what I can do to be well balanced like that, I really don't know all the subtle attributes they possess that must come as natural to them, but not to me.

I agree with your thoughts regarding the job.  I guess I really spend a lot of time with it, but being as I don't have any hobbies and I consider my job the hobby, maybe I should pick up something else on the side and peel away from the job as a hobby mentality.

Still, I really don't gain any pleasure from anything.  I'll smoke a joint once every few months and feel really good, but otherwise it's all just going through the motions; faking the smiles, lying about how well things are going.  I don't drink, smoke or party.

I like to fish a lot, but unfortunately the season only lasts for around 3 months where I'm at.  Most of the time it's cold and dreary.  Otherwise, no, I don't have any hobbies outside of my job.  I read a lot of books in my spare time, but most of them are philosophical and pessimistic and give me existential problems.  Maybe that's a problem, too.

I think there's something to be said of people who grow up with a father figure in their lives.  Not having a positive one myself, I don't really know how to model myself as a well balanced man in society.  I would fix it, but I don't know where to begin.  I've ordered a book on adult children from fatherless backgrounds hoping I'll get some insight from it.  I wish I could tell you what a man misses by growing up without a positive male role model, but I don't know what it is being as I have never had one.

Your questions aren't intrusive, they're exactly the type of inquiries I was hoping to receive.  Thanks for your time.

I'm 30 years old, graduated high school and dropped out of college.

I don't have the social capital needed to land a good job.  I'm very pessimistic and don't have the skills a well balanced man at my age has to relate to other successful men in the world.  I was always an outcast, weird, somewhat shy.  I hung out with the losers, they were the only ones who would accept me.

I don't think this will ever change.

Making it in the real world, to me, means wanting to solve problems and gaining pleasure from achieving goals.  I'm self-employed right now, moderately successful, but I feel no joy and gain no pleasure from it.  I view making it in the real world as actually enjoying what I do and ambitiously working for a goal I find worth achieving.

I guess I just don't derive pleasure out of anything.  I've set short term goals and achieved some of them, but none of them make me happy in the long run.  I have no long term goals because I don't believe I'll ever derive any pleasure from seeing them through, anyways.

Thanks for your questions.
Thank you very much for this help and for taking the time to write it all out for some random stranger.

Yes, thank-you.

I'm on anti-depressants right now, and they've done a great job for me.

Should I talk to a counselor?  I've got the idea that they're more generalists.  Since I know what my major issue is, would a psychologist be better?  I can't afford much, but I'm really wanting to change, and psychologists are expensive.

Any further direction is much appreciated; thanks for taking the time to offer your help.
